quests.definition: Both words describe large size, but large sounds more formal and factual.
quests.example: That is a big deal — we need to celebrate!
quests.usageExample: The elephant is a very large animal.
quests.nativeTip: 'Big' carries emotional weight (big deal, big surprise). 'Large' is neutral, measurable, and factual (large area, large portion).
quests.visualAnchor: 🎉 Big = Emotional | 📊 Large = Factual
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'large mistake' — native speakers always say 'big mistake'.

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: Both words are neutral and interchangeable in almost every situation; 'large' simply sounds a touch more polished in writing.

quests.definition: Both express joy, but glad is usually tied to a specific relief or event.
quests.example: She is a naturally happy person.
quests.usageExample: I am so glad you came to my party.
quests.nativeTip: 'Glad' almost always needs a reason (glad that / glad you called). 'Happy' can stand alone as a state of being.
quests.visualAnchor: ☀️ Happy = General state | 🤝 Glad = Specific reason/relief
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'I am a glad person' — say 'I am a happy person'.

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Glad' is usually followed by a reason (glad that/glad you came), while 'happy' can stand alone to describe a general mood.

quests.definition: Both mean rapid, but quick emphasizes short duration or immediacy.
quests.example: Cheetahs are the fastest land animals.
quests.usageExample: He took a quick shower before work.
quests.nativeTip: 'Fast' refers to speed of motion (fast runner, fast car). 'Quick' refers to an action taking very little time (quick look, quick call).
quests.visualAnchor: 🏎️ Fast = High speed | ⏱️ Quick = Short duration
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'a fast shower' — say 'a quick shower'.

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Quick' leans toward brief actions, while 'fast' more often describes speed of movement itself, like a fast car.

quests.definition: Both mean not difficult, but simple highlights lack of complexity.
quests.example: Passing the quiz was easy after studying.
quests.usageExample: The instructions were simple to follow.
quests.nativeTip: 'Simple' means uncomplicated with few parts. 'Easy' means requiring little effort. Something can be simple but not easy.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧩 Simple = Uncomplicated | 😌 Easy = Low effort
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'a simple test' when you mean 'an easy test'.

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Simple' often highlights a lack of unnecessary parts, while 'easy' focuses on how little effort something takes.

quests.definition: Both mean to commence, but start is conversational while begin is formal.
quests.example: The ceremony will begin promptly at noon.
quests.usageExample: We will start the meeting at 9 AM.
quests.nativeTip: 'Start' is used for physical machines and conversational tasks (start a car, start a business). 'Begin' is preferred in formal or literary writing.
quests.visualAnchor: 📜 Begin = Formal / Ceremony | 🚗 Start = Everyday / Mechanical
quests.commonMistake: Never say 'begin the engine' — always say 'start the engine'.

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Start' is the more common, conversational choice; 'begin' tends to appear in slightly more formal or written English.

quests.definition: Both denote small size, but little carries warmth and affection.
quests.example: He lives in a small apartment downtown.
quests.usageExample: She adopted a little kitten from the shelter.
quests.nativeTip: 'Small' is an objective physical measurement. 'Little' adds emotional affection, sympathy, or triviality (poor little thing).
quests.visualAnchor: 📏 Small = Objective size | 🐶 Little = Affectionate / Cute
quests.commonMistake: Don't use 'little' when presenting formal data or dimensions.

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Little' often carries a warmer, more personal tone than the more neutral 'small.'

quests.definition: Both mean to acquire by paying money, but purchase is commercial and formal.
quests.example: I need to buy some groceries today.
quests.usageExample: I need to purchase a new laptop.
quests.nativeTip: 'Buy' is standard daily speech. 'Purchase' is reserved for legal, corporate, or financial transactions.
quests.visualAnchor: 🛒 Buy = Daily casual | 🧾 Purchase = Formal / Receipts
quests.commonMistake: Saying 'I purchased an apple for snack' sounds overly stiff and unnatural.

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Purchase' sounds more businesslike than 'buy,' which is why it appears in contracts and store policies rather than casual chat.

quests.definition: Both mean low cost, but cheap often implies poor quality.
quests.example: These cheap headphones broke after two days.
quests.usageExample: We found an inexpensive restaurant for lunch.
quests.nativeTip: Calling something 'cheap' can insult its quality or person. Use 'inexpensive' or 'affordable' for good value without poor craftsmanship.
quests.visualAnchor: ⚠️ Cheap = Low price + low quality | 💎 Inexpensive = Affordable + good
quests.commonMistake: Don't tell a friend their gift was 'cheap' unless you mean it's flimsy.

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Inexpensive' avoids the negative undertone 'cheap' can carry, which sometimes suggests poor quality.

quests.definition: Both mean a retail venue; store is American, shop is British.
quests.example: I am heading to the grocery store.
quests.usageExample: She went to the shop to buy some milk.
quests.nativeTip: In US English, almost all retail places are 'stores'. In UK English, 'shop' is preferred for smaller neighborhood retailers.
quests.visualAnchor: 🇺🇸 Store = American standard | 🇬🇧 Shop = British standard
quests.commonMistake: Both are understood globally, but 'shop' in US English often refers to a workshop or boutique.

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Shop' is more common in British English, while 'store' is the everyday choice in American English; both mean the same place.

quests.definition: Both describe good flavor; delicious expresses far higher enthusiasm.
quests.example: This sandwich is quite tasty.
quests.usageExample: The cake was absolutely delicious.
quests.nativeTip: 'Tasty' is a casual compliment (3 out of 5 stars). 'Delicious' is an emphatic 5-star praise used at high-end dining or dinner parties.
quests.visualAnchor: 😋 Tasty = Good & pleasant | 🌟 Delicious = Outstanding flavor
quests.commonMistake: Avoid saying 'very delicious' — delicious is an absolute adjective; say 'absolutely delicious'.

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Delicious' is slightly more enthusiastic than 'tasty,' which is why people reach for it when praising a great meal.

quests.definition: Meal is the entire sitting; dish is a specific prepared recipe item.
quests.example: Breakfast is the most important meal of the day.
quests.usageExample: The chef's signature dish is a spicy noodle soup.
quests.nativeTip: A 'meal' consists of multiple 'dishes' (e.g. appetizer dish, main dish, dessert dish).
quests.visualAnchor: 🍽️ Meal = Complete sitting | 🍲 Dish = Specific recipe
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'My favorite meal is lasagna' — say 'My favorite dish is lasagna'.

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Dish' often refers to one prepared item within a meal, while 'meal' covers the whole sitting, such as dinner.

quests.definition: Cook involves heat; prepare encompasses assembling, chopping, and staging.
quests.example: He loves to cook steak on the grill.
quests.usageExample: She likes to prepare dinner for her family every night.
quests.nativeTip: You 'prepare' a salad (no heat applied). You 'cook' soup or roast chicken (heat applied).
quests.visualAnchor: 🔥 Cook = Applying heat | 🥗 Prepare = Assembling & chopping
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'I cooked a green salad' unless you actually heated the lettuce.

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Prepare' is broader and can include chopping and mixing, not just applying heat, but it's commonly used for cooking overall.

quests.definition: Family usually means the nuclear household; relatives means extended kin.
quests.example: I have dinner with my immediate family every Sunday.
quests.usageExample: All my relatives are coming for Thanksgiving.
quests.nativeTip: 'Family' evokes close emotional bonds. 'Relatives' is a factual designation for aunts, uncles, cousins, and distant kin.
quests.visualAnchor: 👨‍👩‍👧 Family = Close household | 🌳 Relatives = Extended family tree
quests.commonMistake: Don't refer to your spouse as your 'relative'.

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Relatives' is often used for extended family, while 'family' can also mean just parents and siblings.

quests.definition: Kid is casual and conversational; child is formal and proper.
quests.example: The kids are playing soccer in the backyard.
quests.usageExample: The child was playing happily in the park.
quests.nativeTip: Use 'kid' in relaxed chats with friends. Always use 'child' in essays, legal forms, official reports, and news articles.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎈 Kid = Casual & playful | 📚 Child = Formal & academic
quests.commonMistake: Never write 'The kids in the survey' in an academic paper.

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Child' is the neutral, formal term you'd use in writing, while 'kid' is the relaxed version used in conversation.

quests.definition: Marry is everyday speech; wed is poetic or headline journalistic shorthand.
quests.example: Will you marry me?
quests.usageExample: They plan to wed next spring.
quests.nativeTip: Nobody says 'I am going to wed John tomorrow' in casual conversation. 'Wed' is used almost exclusively in newspaper headlines and formal vows.
quests.visualAnchor: 💍 Marry = Real life speech | 📰 Wed = Newspaper headline
quests.commonMistake: Don't propose by saying 'Will you wed me?' — say 'Will you marry me?'

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Wed' is common in formal announcements and news headlines, while 'marry' is used in everyday speech.

quests.definition: Teach is broad and pedagogical; instruct focuses on specific guidelines or drills.
quests.example: She taught me how to read and appreciate literature.
quests.usageExample: The coach will instruct the new players on the rules.
quests.nativeTip: 'Teach' imparts deep understanding and values. 'Instruct' provides procedural orders or step-by-step directions.
quests.visualAnchor: 📖 Teach = Imparting wisdom | 📋 Instruct = Giving clear orders
quests.commonMistake: A pilot doesn't 'teach' passengers to buckle up — they 'instruct' them.

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Instruct' is more formal and often used for structured lessons, while 'teach' fits any situation, formal or casual.

quests.definition: Smart means high general intelligence; clever implies wit or quick ingenuity.
quests.example: He is a smart student with top grades in physics.
quests.usageExample: The clever dog learned a new trick in minutes.
quests.nativeTip: In British English, 'clever' is the standard word for smart. In American English, 'clever' can sometimes imply being tricky or sly.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧠 Smart = General brainpower | 💡 Clever = Ingenious trick / wit
quests.commonMistake: Calling a business scheme 'too clever' in US English can sound like an accusation of cheating.

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Clever' sometimes hints at quick, practical thinking or wit, while 'smart' is the more general, everyday word for intelligence.

quests.definition: Test can be informal or short; exam is comprehensive and high-stakes.
quests.example: We have a quick spelling test every Friday.
quests.usageExample: She passed her final exam with flying colors.
quests.nativeTip: 'Quiz' = tiny (10 mins). 'Test' = regular (1 hour). 'Exam' = milestone or final grade determinant (2-3 hours).
quests.visualAnchor: 📝 Test = Regular evaluation | 🏛️ Exam = Major milestone
quests.commonMistake: Don't call a 3-question pop quiz an 'examination'.

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Exam' usually refers to a bigger, more official test, like a final exam, while 'test' can be small or large.

quests.definition: Job is a countable occupation position; work is the uncountable activity.
quests.example: She applied for three different marketing jobs.
quests.usageExample: He goes to work every morning at eight.
quests.nativeTip: 'Job' is a noun you can count (a job, two jobs). 'Work' is non-countable (you cannot say 'a work' for employment).
quests.visualAnchor: 💼 Job = Specific position (countable) | ⚙️ Work = The effort/tasks (uncountable)
quests.commonMistake: Never say 'I have an important work to do' — say 'I have an important job' or 'important work'.

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Work' can also mean the activity of doing tasks, while 'job' more specifically names the position you hold.

quests.definition: Boss is informal and hierarchical; manager is the official professional title.
quests.example: My boss approved my Friday afternoon off.
quests.usageExample: The manager approved my vacation request.
quests.nativeTip: 'Boss' emphasizes authority and power over you. 'Manager' emphasizes the responsibility of organizing teams and projects.
quests.visualAnchor: 👔 Boss = Authority figure | 📊 Manager = Professional role
quests.commonMistake: In a formal email or resume, refer to your 'manager' or 'supervisor', not your 'boss'.

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Manager' is the official job title, while 'boss' is the informal word employees use in conversation.

quests.definition: Hire is the initial act of taking someone on; employ is the ongoing state.
quests.example: We decided to hire two new graphic designers.
quests.usageExample: The company plans to employ ten new graduates this year.
quests.nativeTip: 'Hire' is an event (to hire on Monday). 'Employ' is a continuous status (employed for five years).
quests.visualAnchor: 🤝 Hire = The hiring event | 🏢 Employ = Continuous workforce
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'The company hires 5,000 workers' when you mean they currently have them on payroll.

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Employ' is often used to describe an ongoing arrangement, while 'hire' focuses on the moment someone joins.

quests.definition: Trip is the whole excursion out and back; journey is the passage or transit time.
quests.example: We went on a weekend camping trip to the mountains.
quests.usageExample: The journey across the desert was long and difficult.
quests.nativeTip: 'Trip' includes going there, staying, and returning. 'Journey' focuses specifically on the travel distance and movement between points.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎒 Trip = Whole vacation / getaway | 🚂 Journey = The transit route
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'How was your journey to Paris?' if you want to ask about their entire vacation.

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Journey' often sounds longer or more meaningful, while 'trip' is the everyday word for any travel, short or long.

quests.definition: Holiday is British for time off or public festivals; vacation is American for leisure trips.
quests.example: They are going on holiday to Spain next week.
quests.usageExample: We are planning a vacation to the coast this summer.
quests.nativeTip: In the US, 'holidays' strictly mean Thanksgiving, Christmas, etc. Time off from work is always 'vacation'.
quests.visualAnchor: 🇬🇧 Holiday = UK time off / festive day | 🇺🇸 Vacation = US time off
quests.commonMistake: If you tell an American 'I went on holiday', they will think you celebrated New Year's or Christmas.

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Vacation' is standard in American English, while 'holiday' is used the same way in British English.

quests.definition: Arrive uses prepositions (at/in); reach is transitive and takes a direct object.
quests.example: Flight 204 will arrive in London at 6:00 PM.
quests.usageExample: We will reach the hotel by noon.
quests.nativeTip: Grammar trap! 'Arrive at the hotel' or 'arrive in Paris' (requires at/in). 'Reach the hotel' or 'reach Paris' (NO preposition!).
quests.visualAnchor: 🛬 Arrive at/in | 🎯 Reach [direct place]
quests.commonMistake: Never say 'reach to the airport' or 'arrive the airport'.

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Reach' often emphasizes the effort of getting somewhere, while 'arrive' simply states that you got there.

quests.definition: Call is universal; ring is distinctively British/Commonwealth.
quests.example: I will call you as soon as the plane lands.
quests.usageExample: I'll ring you later this evening.
quests.nativeTip: 'Ring' is extremely natural in the UK and Australia ('give me a ring', 'ring up the clinic'). 'Call' is standard everywhere.
quests.visualAnchor: 📱 Call = Global standard | ☎️ Ring = British / Commonwealth
quests.commonMistake: In the US, 'give me a ring' might sound like asking for jewelry (a wedding ring) to children!

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Ring' is used mainly in British English for phone calls, while 'call' is understood everywhere.

quests.definition: Message is any written or voice notice; text specifically denotes SMS/chat.
quests.example: Did you receive my voice message on WhatsApp?
quests.usageExample: She sent a quick text to confirm the plans.
quests.nativeTip: 'Text' can be a noun or verb ('text me later'). 'Message' can be email, voice note, letter, or chat.
quests.visualAnchor: ✉️ Message = General communication | 💬 Text = Instant SMS / chat
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'I texted you an audio memo' — say 'I messaged you a voice note'.

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Text' specifically means a message sent by phone, while 'message' is the general word for any communication.

quests.definition: Fix is conversational; repair is formal and technical.
quests.example: Can you fix the loose cabinet handle?
quests.usageExample: The mechanic will repair my car today.
quests.nativeTip: 'Fix' can also mean solve problems ('fix a schedule', 'fix a bug'). 'Repair' refers to restoring physical machinery or structures.
quests.visualAnchor: 🔧 Fix = Casual / Problem-solving | ⚙️ Repair = Professional restoration
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'repair a misunderstanding' — say 'resolve' or 'fix a misunderstanding'.

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Repair' sounds slightly more technical or professional, while 'fix' is the everyday word for the same action.

quests.definition: Sick is common American usage; ill is formal and British.
quests.example: I caught the flu and felt sick all weekend.
quests.usageExample: He felt ill and went home early.
quests.nativeTip: In British English, 'feeling sick' often specifically means feeling nauseous or about to vomit! 'Ill' is used for having a disease.
quests.visualAnchor: 🤒 Sick = American everyday (or nauseous UK) | 🏥 Ill = Formal & UK health
quests.commonMistake: In London, telling someone 'I'm sick' might lead them to hand you a bucket!

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Ill' is common in British English and formal writing, while 'sick' is the everyday word in American English.

quests.definition: Tired is standard low energy; weary implies deep, prolonged mental or physical exhaustion.
quests.example: I am tired after a long day at the desk.
quests.usageExample: After the long shift, the nurse felt weary.
quests.nativeTip: 'Weary' describes deep weariness of body or soul (world-weary). 'Tired' can just mean you need an hour of sleep.
quests.visualAnchor: 🥱 Tired = Need sleep | 🧗 Weary = Bone-deep exhaustion
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'I am weary' just because you woke up 15 minutes early.

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Weary' often implies exhaustion from something long or difficult, while 'tired' can describe any level of low energy.

quests.definition: Doctor is the spoken title; physician is the medical profession designation.
quests.example: I have an appointment to see my doctor on Thursday.
quests.usageExample: The physician examined the patient carefully.
quests.nativeTip: 'Doctor' can refer to PhD holders, dentists, veterinarians. 'Physician' specifically means an MD medical doctor.
quests.visualAnchor: 🩺 Doctor = Conversational | 📜 Physician = Licensed medical MD
quests.commonMistake: Do not call a PhD professor a 'physician'.

rawExtra.nuanceDifference: 'Physician' is used in official or medical contexts, while 'doctor' is the word people use in everyday conversation.
